rows: Let \(I\) be an interval and let \(f: I \to \mathbb{R}\) be a function. We say that \(f\) is increasing if for any \(x_{1}, x_{2} \in I\), \(x_{1} < x_{2} \Rightarrow f(x_{1}) \le f(x_{2})\).
Let \(I\) be an interval and let \(f: I \to \mathbb{R}\) be a function. We say that \(f\) is decreasing if for any \(x_{1}, x_{2} \in I\), \(x_{1} < x_{2} \Rightarrow f(x_{1}) \ge f(x_{2})\).
blocks.caption: Increasing and decreasing functions (as printed in the book)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
In simple words: \(f\) is increasing when its graph never goes down as we move from left to right (a bigger input never gives a smaller output), and decreasing when its graph never goes up.
The book uses \(\le\) and \(\ge\), so a flat piece is allowed. If we want the graph to go strictly up we write \(f(x_{1}) < f(x_{2})\) (strictly increasing), and strictly down \(f(x_{1}) > f(x_{2})\) (strictly decreasing).
The words always refer to an interval: \(f(x) = x^{2}\) is decreasing on \((-\infty, 0]\) and increasing on \([0, \infty)\), but neither on the whole real line.

blocks.title: Recall!
blocks.text: \((a, b)\), \([a, b]\), \((a, b]\), \([a, b)\), \((-\infty, a)\), \((-\infty, \infty)\), \((-\infty, a]\), \((a, \infty)\), \([a, \infty)\) all are intervals.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: An interval is an unbroken piece of the number line. A round bracket leaves the end point out, a square bracket keeps it in; \(\infty\) is never a number, so it always gets a round bracket.
Let \(f\) be a differentiable function defined on an interval \(I\). Then

items: (i) \(f\) is increasing on \(I\), if \(f'(x) \ge 0\) for each \(x \in I\).
(ii) \(f\) is decreasing on \(I\), if \(f'(x) \le 0\) for each \(x \in I\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why does the sign of the derivative decide it? \(f'(x)\) is the slope of the tangent line at \(x\) (2.7).
A positive slope means the tangent, and the curve with it, rises to the right; a negative slope means it falls to the right.
So instead of comparing \(f(x_{1})\) and \(f(x_{2})\) for all pairs (impossible to do one by one), we check one thing: the sign of \(f'(x)\) on the interval.

blocks.title: Example 15
blocks.problem: Prove that \(f(x) = e^{x}\) defined on \(\mathbb{R} = (-\infty, \infty)\) is increasing.
steps:
Given: \(f(x) = e^{x}\) on \((-\infty, \infty)\).
To prove: \(f\) is increasing on \((-\infty, \infty)\).
Method: \(f\) is differentiable, so we use test (i): if \(f'(x) \ge 0\) for every \(x\) in the interval, \(f\) is increasing. We only have to find the sign of \(f'(x)\).

Step 1: Differentiate
\[f'(x) = \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(e^{x}\right) = e^{x}\]
Why: the exponential function \(e^{x}\) is its own derivative (2.5).

Step 2: Find the sign of \(f'(x)\)
\[f'(x) = e^{x} > 0\]
\[\text{for each } x \in (-\infty, \infty)\]
Why: a positive base raised to any real power is positive; \(e \approx 2.718 > 0\), so \(e^{x}\) is never zero or negative.

Step 3: Conclude
Since \(f'(x) > 0\) on the whole real line, \(f(x) = e^{x}\) is increasing on \(\mathbb{R} = (-\infty, \infty)\).
Why: this is test (i) above, and \(> 0\) is even stronger than \(\ge 0\).

Check: take \(x_{1} = 0 < x_{2} = 1\).
\[f(0) = 1 < f(1) = e \approx 2.718\]
The larger input gives the larger output, as the definition requires.
blocks.answer: \(f'(x) = e^{x} > 0\) for every real \(x\), so \(f(x) = e^{x}\) is increasing on \((-\infty, \infty)\).

blocks.title: Example 16
blocks.problem: Show that \(f(x) = 2^{-x}\) defined on \(\mathbb{R} = (-\infty, \infty)\) is decreasing.
steps:
Given: \(f(x) = 2^{-x}\) on \((-\infty, \infty)\).
To show: \(f\) is decreasing on \((-\infty, \infty)\).
Method: test (ii): if \(f'(x) \le 0\) for every \(x\) in the interval, \(f\) is decreasing. We differentiate with the rule for \(a^{u}\) and the chain rule.

Step 1: The book's working
The book writes \(f'(x) = 2^{-x}\frac{d}{dx}(-x) = -2^{-x} < 0\) for each \(x \in (-\infty, \infty)\). The factor \(\ln 2\) is missing (see the Book correction below); the conclusion is still right.
Why we mention it: \(\frac{d}{dx}\left(2^{u}\right) = 2^{u}\ln 2\,\frac{du}{dx}\), not \(2^{u}\frac{du}{dx}\). Only for the base \(e\) does the logarithm factor disappear, because \(\ln e = 1\).

Step 2: Differentiate correctly
\[f'(x) = 2^{-x}\ln 2 \cdot \dfrac{d}{dx}(-x)\]
\[= 2^{-x}\ln 2 \cdot (-1)\]
\[f'(x) = -2^{-x}\ln 2\]
Why: \(\frac{d}{dx}\left(a^{u}\right) = a^{u}\ln a \cdot \frac{du}{dx}\) (2.5) with \(a = 2\) and \(u = -x\), so \(\frac{du}{dx} = -1\).

Step 3: Find the sign of \(f'(x)\)
\[2^{-x} > 0,\quad \ln 2 \approx 0.693 > 0\]
\[f'(x) = -2^{-x}\ln 2 < 0\]
\[\text{for each } x \in (-\infty, \infty)\]
Why: \(2^{-x}\) is positive and \(\ln 2\) is positive (since \(2 > 1\)); the minus sign in front makes the product negative.

Step 4: Conclude
So \(f(x) = 2^{-x}\) is a decreasing function on \(\mathbb{R} = (-\infty, \infty)\).
Why: test (ii).

Check: take \(x_{1} = 0 < x_{2} = 1\).
\[f(0) = 2^{0} = 1 > f(1) = 2^{-1} = \tfrac{1}{2}\]
The larger input gives the smaller output, so \(f\) goes down.
blocks.answer: \(f'(x) = -2^{-x}\ln 2 < 0\) for every real \(x\), so \(f(x) = 2^{-x}\) is decreasing on \((-\infty, \infty)\).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Example 16 prints \(f'(x) = 2^{-x}\frac{d}{dx}(-x)\) and then \(f'(x) = -2^{-x} < 0\). The derivative of \(a^{u}\) is \(a^{u}\ln a\,\frac{du}{dx}\), so the factor \(\ln 2\) is missing. Correct: \(f'(x) = -2^{-x}\ln 2 < 0\). Because \(\ln 2 > 0\), the sign and the conclusion (decreasing) do not change.

blocks.title: Numbering note
blocks.text: The book prints the label "Example 16" twice: here (\(f(x) = 2^{-x}\)) and again under 2.9.1 (\(f(x) = |x|\)). We keep both printed numbers so that every example can be found by its printed label.

blocks.title: Exam tip
blocks.text: For "prove that \(f\) is increasing" questions write three lines: the derivative, its sign with the reason ("since \(e^{x} > 0\) for all \(x\)"), and the conclusion with the interval.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Increasing: \(x_{1} < x_{2} \Rightarrow f(x_{1}) \le f(x_{2})\); decreasing: \(x_{1} < x_{2} \Rightarrow f(x_{1}) \ge f(x_{2})\).
2. For a differentiable \(f\): \(f'(x) \ge 0\) on \(I\) gives increasing, \(f'(x) \le 0\) on \(I\) gives decreasing.
3. Always name the interval: a function can increase on one interval and decrease on another.
4. \(e^{x}\) is increasing on \(\mathbb{R}\); \(2^{-x} = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{x}\) is decreasing on \(\mathbb{R}\).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Forgetting the factor \(\ln a\) when differentiating \(a^{x}\): \(\frac{d}{dx}\left(2^{-x}\right) = -2^{-x}\ln 2\), not \(-2^{-x}\).
2. Saying "\(f\) is increasing" without an interval.
3. Checking the sign of \(f(x)\) instead of \(f'(x)\): \(2^{-x}\) is always positive, yet it is decreasing.
